summary: This Wikipedia-style note defines biological immortality as a state where mortality from senescence is stable or decreasing with age, and notes that biologically immortal beings can still die from injury, disease, predation or other causes. It covers the term's use for cell lines not subject to the Hayflick limit (HeLa, Jurkat, telomerase-expressing cancer cells), and surveys organisms that show negligible aging, including Hydra, Turritopsis jellyfish, lobsters, and planarian flatworms, along with bacteria and yeast that can reset under ideal conditions.
one_line: Overview of biological immortality, covering the senescence-based definition, immortal cell lines, and organisms with negligible aging such as hydra, jellyfish, lobsters and planarians.
key_facts: Biological immortality is a state in which the rate of mortality from senescence is stable or decreasing, decoupling it from chronological age.
A biologically immortal living being can still die from injury, poison, disease, predation, lack of resources, or changes to environment.
The late-life mortality plateau idea challenges the definition of immortality, because the increase in mortality with chronological age may be negligible at extremely old ages.
Biologists chose the word "immortal" to designate cells not subject to the Hayflick limit, the point at which cells can no longer divide due to DNA damage or shortened telomeres.
Alexis Carrel hypothesized that all normal somatic cells were immortal, prior to Leonard Hayflick's theory.
HeLa and Jurkat are among the most commonly used immortalized cancer cell lines, used in research such as creation of the polio vaccine.
According to the Animal Aging and Longevity Database, the Greenland shark has an estimated longevity of 250 to 500 years in the wild.
The ocean quahog clam (Arctica islandica) has an estimated wild longevity of 507 years.

In 2018, scientists working for Calico, a company owned by Alphabet, published a paper in eLife presenting possible evidence that the naked mole rat does not face increased mortality risk due to aging.
Symmetrically dividing bacteria and yeast can be biologically immortal under ideal growing conditions, while asymmetrically budding parents are not restored and go on to age and die.
Hydras are simple freshwater animals; all hydra cells continually divide, and in a four-year study three cohorts did not show an increase in mortality with age.
Turritopsis dohrnii is a jellyfish about 5 millimeters (0.20 in) long that uses transdifferentiation to replenish cells after sexual reproduction, a cycle that can repeat indefinitely.
Lobsters express telomerase as adults through most tissue, unlike most vertebrates, which may be related to their longevity, but lobsters are not immortal and often die during a moult.
The European lobster has an average life span of 31 years for males and 54 years for females.
Asexual planarians of the genus Schmidtea mediterranea maintain telomere length somatically, while sexual planarians can live as long as 3 years.
Asexual planarian clonal lines replicating by fission have been maintained for over 15 years.
